html:
Update, 2026-11-16: both next steps at the end of this post are done. A routed model call proved the logs row on 2026-11-15, and it showed that the check's own log queries had been looking in the wrong place: a mark's name is stored as structured metadata, not in the text of the record, so the old filters always counted zero. The gateway now runs Relay's newer release, and the Capture tab shows what it adds: the gateway process's CPU, memory, open files and disk, and the routing plugin's requests, failures and overhead, for every role, plus Relay's runtime diagnostics as counts and codes for admins. All of it is on main and still not in a tagged release.

NeMo Relay is the gateway my coding agents talk to. Requests from opencode, and from Claude Code when I launch it through Relay, pass through it on their way to a model, and Relay can write down what happened: each lifecycle event, a trajectory per session, and OpenTelemetry spans in more than one shape. Until this week I recorded the smallest useful set. Two things were missing: more of what Relay can capture, and somewhere to actually read it.

What Relay can record, and what I had on

Relay records at several levels at once. The raw one is ATOF, a JSON line per event on disk. ATIF is one trajectory file per session. On top of those it exports OpenTelemetry spans in three projections (the standard gen_ai conventions, OpenInference, and Relay's own full shape), plus logs and metrics. I had been exporting gen_ai spans and metrics, with payloads filtered down to the newest turn.

That filtering mattered more than I expected. In a throwaway gateway with a fake upstream, three calls in one session carrying 2, 4 and 6 messages were recorded as 2, 2 and 2: the system prompt plus the newest message. The history the model actually saw was gone from the record. With complete payloads on, the same three calls were recorded as 2, 4 and 6.

I now name the choices as levels and apply them with one script, which validates a candidate config in an isolated directory, backs up the live one, restarts the gateway and checks its banner:

beforeenrichedfull (live now)
ATOF events and ATIF trajectories on diskyesyesyes
What a model call keepsnewest turncomplete requestcomplete request
gen_ai spans to Tempoyesyes, plus Relay's metadatasame
OpenInference spans to Phoenixnonoyes
Relay's marks (routing decisions, hook events) as logsnonoyes
PII redaction before every sinkyesyesyes

Relay's own full projection is the one level I left off on purpose. It carries what ATOF already carries and none of the attributes a trace store renders, so no viewer here would show it better than the projections they already get.

Two copies of one span

Turning on a second projection had a catch. Both copies of a span share the same trace and span ids, so sending both to one store makes them collide. The OpenTelemetry collector now routes them: gen_ai to Tempo, OpenInference to Phoenix. I have Relay tag each projection with a resource attribute, and the rule that removes the gen_ai copy from Phoenix also requires a second tag that only the full level sends. Without that guard, rolling back to a lower level would have left Phoenix with no Relay spans at all. A review of the script by a reviewer that had not written it caught the missing guard before anything was applied.

A test marker that redaction ate

The script has a verify step that sends one synthetic request and looks for it in every store, with a positive control for every negative claim: "Tempo holds no OpenInference copy" only counts if this run's gen_ai span is in Tempo. Its first live run failed. The span was there, but its name ended in [REDACTED-PHONE]: the marker was letters plus a ten-digit timestamp, and Relay's PII redaction did its job on a digit run that looks like a phone number in the OpenTelemetry exports. The marker is letters only now. Separately, one fixed wait turned out to be too short for Tempo to make the span searchable, so that check now polls for up to 90 seconds. Today verify proves that Tempo has the gen_ai span and no OpenInference copy, and that Phoenix has the OpenInference span. The logs row needs one routed model call and is next on the list.

A place to read it

NVIDIA's own tutorial uses Arize Phoenix to visualise Relay's traces, and Phoenix now gets its native format. But the record I trust most is the ATOF stream on disk, and the questions I ask most are about Relay specifically: which route did a request take, how did a session's context grow, where did a tool call stall. So Nemo Console, my open-source console for the NVIDIA stack in my lab, gained five tabs on its Relay page that read Relay's own files.

  • Traces: a filterable list, and per trace a waterfall, an icicle and a span table that share one selection, with the routing decision, tokens, time to first chunk and the chunk cadence of every model call.
  • Sessions: every trace of an agent session on one timeline, and the context the model was given call by call, cached and uncached.
  • Analytics: totals, latency and token series, histograms, an activity heatmap, routing flows, tools and errors.
  • Trajectories: Relay's own trajectories and those my Hermes agents write, step by step.
  • Capture: which capture levels are on, what was observed for each, and what a reader of the traces is missing.

The design is the part I would keep for any tool like this. One background task reads the files into an in-memory index, incrementally: it remembers each file's identity and how far it has read, re-reads a file that was truncated in place, and never counts a rotated copy twice. The index holds metadata only: identifiers, numbers and timestamps. Prompts, completions and tool payloads are never stored in the index or returned by the views a read-only key can open. They are read from the source line on demand, by two routes that need an admin key, can be switched off, scrub known secret patterns and return only a fixed list of headers.

A test plants one marker string in every payload field of the fixtures: messages, tool arguments, tool results, streamed chunks, headers, trajectory steps. It calls every read-only route and asserts the marker never appears, then calls the admin route and asserts it does. A check that the marker is absent proves nothing unless the same test can find it where it should be.

What real data found

The fixtures were synthetic and passed. The first run against my real captures (2.4 GiB in seven files, four of them gzip rotations: about 566,000 events, 1,900 traces and 840 trajectories) found four problems none of them had:

  • Every Hermes trajectory was skipped. Their ids are not UUIDs, and the code assumed they were. They now get a stable id derived from the original, which stays visible.
  • Opening a span from an old rotation was slow in proportion to its depth. Near the end of a 1 GB gzip file it took 54 seconds, because gzip has no random access. The index now records seek points while it reads a rotation (the decompressor's state roughly every 32 MiB of output), and a read resumes from the nearest one. The deepest read dropped below one second (both numbers from a debug build).
  • Credentials inside tool output needed their own pass. Content now gets an extra pass for secret-named pairs in JSON, YAML and environment-file form.
  • One 494-trace session needed about a hundred lanes on its timeline. The timeline now keeps twelve lanes and says how many short traces overlap.

With the release build the first index of all of it takes about 15 seconds and the console holds about 100 MB; after that, refreshes take milliseconds.

A security review before merging

Nemo Console is public, and these views open conversation content, so a reviewer with no part in writing the change read it before it merged, then re-read the fixes twice. It found nothing critical, one medium issue and four low ones, all addressed before the merge (two smaller limits are documented in the threat model rather than changed). The lessons generalise:

  • A scrubber should not depend on an engine that can give up. Secret scrubbing now runs only on linear-time regular expressions. A test checks the new pattern against the old one over 400 generated texts, and the re-review compared it with the original Python pattern on 60,000 random texts without a single difference.
  • Budgets must count what you actually decompress, not what a file declares.
  • Bound every collection, not just the obvious one. Spans were capped; marks and interned identifiers now are too.
  • Re-check a file when you read it, not only when you index it. A changed trajectory is now refused instead of served.

The re-review also caught a regression in my first fix, which is why the final fix replaced the engine instead of adding a fallback.

Where it stands

The trace views and the review's fixes are merged to main and running here (not yet in a tagged release), with the release gates, the browser suite and the comparison against the old Python backend all green. Relay records at full. Next comes the routed call that proves the logs row. After that, possibly the upgrade to Relay's newer release, which adds resource metrics and runtime diagnostics the Capture tab could show.
